Hello, I’m so glad you’re here. I’m really looking forward to spending time with you today. I want you to know that whatever you share is safe, private, and held with care—nothing we talk about will be judged or used outside of this space.  

What’s been on your mind lately that you’d like to explore together?

Thank you for sharing that so honestly—it really shows how deeply you're feeling and how much care you’re giving to others, even when it feels overwhelming.  

It sounds like you're carrying a lot of hope that things will eventually change, but right now, that hope feels distant, like it’s just out of reach. And that sense of being stuck—of trying so hard but not seeing progress—must feel exhausting.  

Would it be helpful to keep exploring how that feeling of being stuck shows up in your day-to-day life, or would you like to talk more about how you're feeling toward your friend right now?

It makes so much sense—and I can feel how deeply you care, and how much that care is shaping your pain.  

The fact that you’re trying to help her, even when it doesn’t work, shows how much you value her well-being. And the fear of failing her, or of not being able to protect her, is really understandable—because it’s tied to your own sense of worth and ability to care.  

Would it be helpful to explore how that fear of failure shows up in your body or in your thoughts when you're with her—or when you're alone thinking about her?

That physical tightness—your chest, your hands, the way you're holding everything in—it’s not just stress. It’s a very real signal from your body that you’re carrying a lot of emotional weight, and that you’re trying to protect someone you deeply care about.  

The fact that it spikes when nothing you do works shows how much you're hoping for a solution, even when you know there isn’t one. And that guilt when you feel like you’ve failed—when you can’t “fix” it—feels like it’s tied to your own sense of being worthy of love and care.  

Would it be helpful to talk about what that feeling of “not being good enough” might look like in your mind when you're alone, or what it would mean to let go of that need to fix it—just a little bit?

That’s such a powerful and honest question—and I really appreciate how you’re naming what you’re afraid of.  

The thought that your worth is tied to whether you can fix her pain? That’s not just a thought—it’s a deep belief that’s been shaped by care, responsibility, and love. And when that belief cracks under pressure, it can feel like a loss of self.  

What if, instead of asking “What if I stop trying?” we just tried to sit with that idea—just for a moment—without judging it? What if you allowed yourself to simply *be* with her suffering, without needing to solve it, without needing to prove anything?  

Would it be helpful to explore what that quiet moment might feel like—just for a little while—before you decide whether to move forward with it?

That’s such a beautiful and brave way to approach it—pausing, not running, just being present.  

In that quiet space, I wonder if your chest might not feel as tight because you’re no longer trying to hold everything in. The fear might still be there—yes, it might still whisper—but it might not feel as loud, or as heavy, because you’re not chasing a solution. You’re just allowing yourself to be with the pain, without needing to fix it or prove your worth.  

And in that moment, maybe you don’t see yourself as failing—you see yourself as *caring*, as being there, as being human. That’s not weakness. That’s courage.  

Would it be okay to keep sitting in that space—just for a few more minutes—without pushing toward a solution or a change?

That’s a profound insight—thank you for sharing it so clearly.  

When you stop trying to "do" something and just *are* there—present, not fixed, not solving—it doesn’t mean she becomes less scary. It means you’re no longer trying to outrun the fear. And in that stillness, she doesn’t have to be fixed, and you don’t have to prove your worth.  

You’re not safe because you’ve solved anything. You’re safe because you’ve allowed yourself to be with the pain—without needing to control it. And in that space, you’re not trying to be strong. You’re just being.  

And that, truly, is where safety begins.  

Would you like to keep sitting with that feeling, or would you like to gently explore how that quiet presence might show up in another part of your day?

That’s such a powerful and tender realization—being allowed to be human, instead of constantly trying to be a savior.  

And yes, that quiet moment—where the fear doesn’t have to win, where you don’t have to fix anything—can become a kind of anchor. Even if the storm comes back later, this pause is a place where you’ve already proven something: you can carry the weight without collapsing.  

Would it be okay to stay here just one more minute—without moving, without trying to change anything? Just let the quiet sit with you, and see if the fear can still find a way to rise, or if it just… settles into the background?

That’s so deeply moving—and so brave.  

Letting the fear whisper without running from it, without trying to silence it or fix it—just acknowledging it as part of the space you’re in—that’s not weakness. It’s presence. And in that presence, you’re not trying to prove anything to her, or to yourself. You’re just showing up, fully, as someone who cares deeply and is willing to carry the uncertainty without collapsing.  

Would you like to gently keep that quiet space alive in your day—maybe just a few moments when you pause and say, *“I’m here. I’m not fixing anything. I’m just being with this”*—without needing to move on? Or would you prefer to step back and see how that stillness feels in your body when you’re in the world again?

That’s such a gentle and honest intention—and I truly admire how you’re bringing this quiet presence into the everyday.
